title: Study of Compounds: Nitric Acid
tagline: The acid that is more oxidiser than acid: concentrated action, passive iron and the Ostwald route.

overview.intro: Nitric acid breaks the pattern the other acids set. Yes it neutralises bases, but its most distinctive behaviour is as an oxidising acid: concentrated nitric acid attacks metals without giving hydrogen at all, oxidises the hydrogen it would otherwise release, and makes iron passive. This chapter covers its laboratory preparation, the storage problem that forces amber bottles, the difference between dilute and concentrated reactions, and the industrial Ostwald process that supplies the world’s nitric acid.

facts.label: Preparation
facts.value: Sodium or potassium nitrate heated with concentrated sulphuric acid.

facts.label: Oxidising character
facts.value: Concentrated nitric acid gives brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide as it is reduced.

facts.label: Passivity
facts.value: Concentrated acid forms a protective oxide film on iron and aluminium.

facts.label: Storage
facts.value: Kept in amber bottles because light decomposes it to nitrogen dioxide.

learningOutcomes: Describe the laboratory preparation of nitric acid and explain why glass apparatus and amber bottles are used.
State the physical properties of nitric acid including its decomposition in light.
Compare the reactions of dilute and concentrated nitric acid with metals and with non-metals.
Explain passivity and give one practical application of it.
Outline the Ostwald process and the uses of nitric acid in explosives, fertilisers and refining.

blocks.text: Laboratory preparation displaces the more volatile nitric acid from its salt with concentrated sulphuric acid, exactly the pattern used for hydrogen chloride. Potassium nitrate or sodium nitrate is warmed with the concentrated acid, and nitric acid distils over because it is the more volatile of the two. Two properties dictate the apparatus. First, the acid attacks cork and rubber, so all joints must be glass-to-glass, which is unusual in school preparations and is a favourite examination detail. Second, the product must be collected in a glass flask and stored in an amber bottle, because nitric acid decomposes when struck by light into water, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen, and the brown gas dissolves to give the yellowish-brown colour of an old sample. Pure nitric acid is colourless; colour in the bottle is a sign of decomposition, not of impurity alone.

items: Reagents: concentrated sulphuric acid with sodium or potassium nitrate, warmed gently.
Apparatus is all glass because the acid corrodes rubber and cork.
The acid distils over since it is more volatile than sulphuric acid.
Stored in amber bottles, filled to reduce the air space, because light causes decomposition.
The preparation equation to memorise: KNO3 + H2SO4 → KHSO4 + HNO3, warmed gently so the nitric acid distils over before it decomposes.
Decomposition in light is written 4HNO3 → 4NO2 + O2 + 2H2O, which explains both the brown colour and why amber glass is used.

items.text: Colour change in an old bottle
items.note: A sample turning yellow-brown has partly decomposed, giving dissolved nitrogen dioxide.
A rubber connector joining the flask to the delivery tube would be charred and pitted by the vapour.

items.meaning: Brown glass bottle that filters out light and prevents photochemical decomposition.
Readiness to evaporate; nitric acid is more volatile than sulphuric acid and is displaced.
Loss of chemical activity of a metal through formation of a protective oxide film.

learn.title: Why nitric acid oxidises instead of simply donating protons

blocks.text: When a metal reacts with a typical acid, hydrogen ions accept electrons and hydrogen gas escapes. Nitric acid takes a different path because the nitrate ion itself is a powerful oxidising agent: instead of hydrogen being released, the hydrogen that forms is immediately oxidised to water while nitrogen in the nitrate is reduced. With dilute acid the reduction usually gives nitric oxide, a colourless gas that turns brown on contact with air; with concentrated acid the reduction stops earlier at nitrogen dioxide, the dense brown fumes that define the reaction. The products therefore depend on concentration, which is why a question about "the reaction of nitric acid with copper" is never complete without stating which concentration was meant. Even hydrogen-evolving reactions are rare, and that single exception — very dilute acid with magnesium — only confirms the rule.

items: Nitric acid does not normally liberate hydrogen from metals, because the hydrogen is oxidised to water.
Dilute acid with copper gives colourless nitric oxide, which browns on contact with air.
Concentrated acid with copper gives brown nitrogen dioxide directly.
The nitrate ion is reduced while the metal is oxidised, so the acid supplies both the oxidant and the acid character.
Cu + 4HNO3 (conc.) → Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO2 + 2H2O, which is why the brown fumes appear above a blue-green solution.
With dilute acid the reduction stops higher: 3Cu + 8HNO3 (dil.) → 3Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO + 4H2O, and the colourless NO browns in air.

items.note: Copper gives copper(II) nitrate and nitric oxide; the gas turns brown above the solution as it meets air.
Rapid reaction gives brown nitrogen dioxide and a blue-green solution of copper(II) nitrate.

blocks.text: Concentrated nitric acid does something peculiar with iron and aluminium: at first it reacts sharply, then the reaction stops completely. The acid oxidises the surface to a tough, insoluble oxide film that blocks further contact between metal and acid, and the metal is said to be passive. This is not a coating that can be scraped off and forgotten — the film reforms instantly in air — and it has a practical use: concentrated nitric acid can be shipped in aluminium tankers because the metal passivates as soon as the acid touches it. With non-metals the same oxidising power appears as combustion without flame: carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide, sulphur to sulphuric acid and phosphorus to phosphoric acid. Finally, when hydrochloric and nitric acids are mixed three to one, the resulting aqua regia dissolves gold and platinum through a combination of chloride complexation and nitrate oxidation.

items: Passivity: a thin, tough oxide layer forms on iron or aluminium and stops the reaction.
Aluminium tankers carry concentrated nitric acid safely because the surface passivates immediately.
Carbon oxidises to carbon dioxide and sulphur to sulphuric acid with hot concentrated acid.
Aqua regia, three parts hydrochloric to one part nitric, dissolves gold by oxidising it into a chloride complex.

items.text: Iron immersed in concentrated nitric acid
items.note: Initial effervescence ceases at once; a piece of passive iron then cannot displace copper solution.
The sulphur is oxidised to sulphuric acid while nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide.

items.meaning: Iron rendered unreactive by an oxide film formed by a strong oxidising acid.
Acid that supplies oxygen or accepts electrons itself, as nitric acid does.
Three-to-one mixture of concentrated hydrochloric and nitric acids that dissolves gold.

blocks.text: Nearly all nitric acid is made by oxidising ammonia rather than by distilling it from a salt. In the first step ammonia is mixed with air and passed over a platinum-rhodium catalyst at about 800 °C, where it oxidises to nitric oxide. The gas is cooled and oxidised again in air to give nitrogen dioxide, and that brown gas is then absorbed in water under pressure, where it disproportionates to give nitric acid and some nitric oxide which is recycled. Every stage is chosen to keep the nitrogen moving forward: the catalyst makes the first oxidation fast at a practical temperature, cooling lets the second oxidation proceed since it is favoured by lower temperature, and absorption under pressure pushes the equilibrium towards acid. The plant reuses the unconverted gas, which is why modern processes achieve high yield with little waste.

items: Step one: catalytic oxidation of ammonia with air over platinum-rhodium near 800 °C giving nitric oxide.
Step two: nitric oxide plus oxygen gives nitrogen dioxide, favoured by cooling.
Step three: absorption in water under pressure gives nitric acid, with nitric oxide recycled.
Overall, the process converts ammonia’s nitrogen all the way to nitrate efficiently and continuously.
The three stage equations: 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O, then 2NO + O2 → 2NO2, then 3NO2 + H2O → 2HNO3 + NO with the NO recycled.

items.note: Platinum-rhodium survives the high temperature and resists poisoning, unlike less robust metals.
Higher pressure drives the gas into solution and shifts the absorbing equilibrium towards the acid.

learn.title: Uses of nitric acid and answering description questions

blocks.text: Nitric acid is one of the industrial pillars because it supplies both nitrate ions and oxidising power. Ammonium nitrate is a major fertiliser and also the oxidiser in many blasting agents; nitroglycerine and trinitrotoluene are made by nitrating organic compounds with the acid; dyes and plastics such as nylon require nitrated intermediates; and the metal refining industry uses the acid to dissolve base metals from ores and scrap. In the laboratory it is the standard acid for dissolving metals before cation tests, and it is never used when a non-oxidising acid is needed — that role belongs to hydrochloric or sulphuric acid. For examination answers, describe each use with the property behind it: nitrating ability for explosives, oxidising power for refining, and the ammonium salt for fertiliser.

items: Fertilisers: ammonium nitrate supplies nitrogen in two plant-available forms.
Explosives: nitroglycerine and TNT are nitrated compounds made with concentrated nitric acid.
Metal refining and qualitative analysis: dissolves metals and keeps the cation in solution for testing.
Dyes, plastics and pharmaceuticals: nitrating steps are built into many organic syntheses.

items.note: Toluene is nitrated by a mixture of nitric and sulphuric acids, introducing nitro groups onto the ring.
Dilute nitric acid dissolves both, and the separate cation tests then distinguish them in solution.

items.meaning: Introduction of a nitro group into an organic compound using nitric acid.
Explosive mixture in which nitrate supplies the oxygen for its own rapid oxidation.
Brown glass that blocks light and prevents decomposition of light-sensitive reagents.

keyPoints: Nitric acid is prepared by warming sodium or potassium nitrate with concentrated sulphuric acid.
The apparatus is all glass because the acid attacks rubber and cork.
Pure nitric acid is colourless but turns yellow-brown on standing in light because it decomposes.
Concentrated nitric acid is stored in amber bottles to exclude light.
It behaves as an oxidising acid: hydrogen formed from a metal is oxidised to water instead of escaping.
Dilute acid with copper gives nitric oxide; concentrated acid gives nitrogen dioxide.
Iron and aluminium become passive in concentrated nitric acid because a protective oxide film forms.
Aqua regia, three parts hydrochloric acid to one part nitric acid, dissolves gold.
The Ostwald process oxidises ammonia over platinum-rhodium, then air, then absorbs the oxide in water.
Uses: fertilisers, explosives, dyes, plastics and metal refining.
examFocus: Never answer a reaction with metal without naming the concentration — dilute and concentrated give different products.
Passivity needs the mechanism: oxide film, not merely the statement that the reaction stops.
The all-glass apparatus and amber bottle facts are two separate marks in a preparation question.
Ostwald is three numbered stages; write each with its reagents and conditions.

vocabulary.meaning: Acid that oxidises the substance it attacks, as nitric acid does through nitrate.
Behaviour of a metal rendered unreactive by a protective oxide film.
Addition of a nitro group to an organic molecule using nitric acid.
Light-excluding brown bottle used for photosensitive reagents.
Tendency to vaporise, exploited to distil nitric acid from its salt.
Brown toxic gas NO2 formed when concentrated nitric acid is reduced.
Three-to-one mixture of concentrated hydrochloric and nitric acids.
Substance added to soil to supply nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium.

questions.prompt: Concentrated nitric acid with copper gives:
questions.explanation: The nitrate ion is reduced to nitrogen dioxide, the dense brown fumes seen above the solution.

questions.prompt: Nitric acid is stored in an amber bottle because:
questions.explanation: Light causes decomposition into water, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen, which colours the acid brown.

questions.prompt: Iron becomes passive in concentrated nitric acid because:
options: The acid freezes on the surface
The iron is coated with nitrate
questions.explanation: The acid oxidises the surface to an insoluble oxide layer that prevents further contact with the metal.

questions.prompt: In the Ostwald process the first step converts ammonia to nitric oxide using:
questions.explanation: Platinum-rhodium catalyses the high-temperature oxidation of ammonia to nitric oxide.

questions.prompt: The laboratory preparation of nitric acid uses concentrated sulphuric acid and a nitrate of sodium or __________.
questions.explanation: Either nitrate works; the less volatile acid displaces the more volatile nitric acid on warming.

questions.prompt: Concentrated __________ acid renders iron passive by building a protective oxide film on its surface.
questions.explanation: The acid oxidises the metal surface to an insoluble oxide layer that blocks any further reaction.

questions.prompt: Why is all-glass apparatus used in the preparation of nitric acid?
questions.answer: Nitric acid vapour attacks rubber and cork, corroding them and contaminating the product, so every connection in the train must be glass to glass to keep the preparation pure and the apparatus intact.
questions.explanation: The corrosive oxidising vapour would destroy organic jointing materials within minutes.

questions.prompt: Explain why nitric acid does not usually liberate hydrogen from metals.
questions.answer: Although hydrogen ions are reduced at the metal surface, the nitrate ion is such a strong oxidising agent that it oxidises the hydrogen to water, while the nitrate itself is reduced to nitrogen oxide. Hydrogen therefore never escapes as a gas, and the usual effervescence of hydrogen is absent.
questions.explanation: The acid supplies an alternative oxidant that consumes the hydrogen as quickly as it forms.

questions.prompt: State what is observed when concentrated nitric acid is poured onto copper.
questions.answer: Dense brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide are evolved, the metal dissolves, and a blue-green solution of copper(II) nitrate remains.
questions.explanation: The brown colour identifies nitrogen dioxide, the reduction product of concentrated acid.

questions.prompt: Describe the Ostwald manufacture of nitric acid, giving the conditions of each stage and one reason for them.
questions.answer: Ammonia is mixed with air and passed over a platinum-rhodium catalyst at about 800 °C, where it oxidises to nitric oxide: 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O. The gases are cooled and passed through more air so that nitric oxide combines with oxygen to give nitrogen dioxide, a step favoured by lower temperature. The brown gas is then absorbed in water under pressure, where it forms nitric acid together with some nitric oxide which is recycled back to the oxidation stage. The catalyst is chosen for activity and durability at high temperature, cooling maximises the second conversion, and pressure drives absorption to completion.
questions.explanation: Three stages with a reason each: catalytic oxidation, cooling oxidation and pressurised absorption.

questions.prompt: Compare the action of dilute and concentrated nitric acid on copper and on iron.
questions.answer: With copper, dilute nitric acid gives copper(II) nitrate and nitric oxide, a colourless gas that browns in air; concentrated acid gives copper(II) nitrate and nitrogen dioxide, dense brown fumes, because the stronger oxidant is reduced only one step further. With iron, dilute acid reacts steadily to give iron(II) nitrate and hydrogen oxide products, while concentrated acid renders the metal passive almost at once by building an insoluble oxide film that stops further attack. Concentration therefore controls both the reduction product of the acid and whether a metal reacts at all.
questions.explanation: Concentration decides how far the nitrate is reduced and whether the oxide film can form before the metal dissolves.

questions.prompt: A metal is found to be unreactive towards concentrated nitric acid but reacts readily with dilute hydrochloric acid. Explain the difference, and predict what would happen if the passive metal were then dipped into copper(II) sulphate solution.
questions.answer: The concentrated acid passivates the metal, forming a tough, insoluble oxide film that separates the surface from the acid and halts the reaction; this does not mean the metal is unreactive in general. Hydrochloric acid is non-oxidising and cannot build such a film, so it attacks the metal normally and releases hydrogen. If the still-passive piece were placed in copper(II) sulphate, it would not displace copper while the film remains intact, because the film blocks electron transfer; once the film is removed by scratching or by acid that dissolves oxides, the metal would displace copper and the blue colour would fade.
questions.explanation: Passivity is a surface phenomenon controlled by the acid’s oxidising power, not an intrinsic property of the metal.
